you might say, and so Ed Naylor and myself made and another notable fact was that Ed Naylor and myself made our first date with Pamela and Lissie and accompanied them out to some kind of entertainment. The time of this story begins necessarily made more and not at the announcement of the 'suspension of rules'—and that announcement was more stirring to the students than the making of dates. For some occasions, such as for 'exhibitions' and scheduled holidays, the suspension of rules was anticipated for some time in advance. Sometimes, for unexpected occasions, the announcement was a partial surprise, and I informed me that she would inform me that she had to go to be off and I could not find my hat. I called to my mother to find it for me and she informed me that my older sister, Roberta, and Miss Nausica Brown had gone out to spend the night with Miss [?] of Mecting, and in those days we boys all had to have a hat or we dared not dressed up.

Well, your mother will remember the 'walking hat'—the hat always fashioned from the hat shop in Denison. My mother got it and tried on the brim of my hat. The mother got it and turned the brim down with a needle and thread. Then I put it on again, viewed it critically—took another look at it in the mirror, and off it came! I pulled the thread, re-sewed the crown, and then turned the brim down carefully to stiff position. I took another look and it fits. So I went and met the young ladies at the door with hat in place. Do you see the situation? I had a 'walking hat' too.

Unfortunately, not all escapes were so watchful eyes, as Mr. Barlow Roberts, of Sherman, recalls in this account:

"I obeyed all the rules of that fine school except one. I was invited to a small private party. I thought it was, one evening to study our grammar lesson. I could not quite see why I should be invited to a little something must go wrong, and little things assume large proportions in the mind of a young man. So I was looking for some escape and I learned that 'old Boy' was sitting on his folded feet just enjoying the fish with us."

And so the story—which it concerned—as it concerned to the annals of 'first-dates'; for the principal in the following episode identified himself, as he labeled in the poem, and the poet has enriched with some experience. The lines are from a Platonian Messenger:

IDENTITY

She was a handsome visitor,
And he was a bright young Prof.!
They met that morn to say farewell
For she was going off—

³Personal letter from Mr. M. H. (Shel Boy) Noel, Dallas, Texas, July 1, 1938.
